title: Area VII review: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
intro: These questions mix the nine ASEL Tasks of Area VII: normal, soft-field and short-field takeoffs and landings, slips, go-arounds and the power-off 180. Most put two Tasks into one real instructing moment, such as a wet grass strip with trees, a slip that turns into a go-around, or a LAHSO offer before an accuracy approach.

questions.q: After a week of rain you and a learner plan to leave a 2,600-foot grass strip: long wet grass, a few soft spots, trees past the far end. She briefs: "Short runway and trees, so short-field technique: start at the very end, roll in a low-drag attitude with the weight on the mains, rotate near VX." What do you teach?
options: Use the soft-field technique: keep rolling, hold back pressure to lighten the nosewheel, lift off slowly, stay in ground effect to VX, then VX until past the trees
Her plan is right: the trees make it an obstacle departure, and the low-drag roll with the weight on the mains gives the shortest ground run on any surface, wet grass or pavement
Use the soft-field roll, but right after lift-off climb at the steepest attitude she can hold, because clearing the trees matters more than airspeed in the first few seconds
Use her short-field plan, but hold the brakes longer at full power on the grass so the engine is fully developed and the wet grass costs less of the runway
questions.why: On a soft surface or in long wet grass, a normal technique may never reach takeoff speed, and the AFH calls the soft-field procedure quite different from the short-field one on a firm, smooth surface [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], where the airplane rolls with its full weight on the main wheels [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. So: keep moving while lining up (stopping can bog the airplane down), hold back pressure, let it fly off below safe climb speed, stay in ground effect until at least VX, then VX until the obstacle is cleared and VY after that [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Climbing steeply out of ground effect too slow gives much less climb than VX, and hot, high or heavy the airplane may not climb out at all [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. Holding the brakes on wet grass is the stop that bogs it down. And the RMH accident on a wet turf strip with trees had no POH data for that surface [[30:64|RMH C-1]], so brief extra margin, not a guess.

questions.q: Before a short-field landing lesson at a dry grass strip, your learner works the 172R short-field landing chart for 2,000 feet pressure altitude, 20 °C and zero wind: 605 feet ground roll, 1,375 feet to clear 50 feet. For the grass note she writes 1,375 x 1.45 = 1,994 feet total. What do you teach?
options: Her 1,994 feet is right: the grass note raises every figure on the chart by 45 percent, so the total over the obstacle grows by the same 45 percent as the ground roll does
About 877 feet total: on grass only the ground roll matters, so the total is the ground roll times 1.45, and the air distance from 50 feet drops out of the planning
About 1,647 feet total: the note adds 45 percent of the ground roll figure, 272 feet, to each distance, and the number still assumes the POH technique and maximum braking
About 1,375 feet total: grass drag shortens the roll about as much as the weaker braking lengthens it, so the paved figure can be used as it is on a dry grass strip
questions.why: Note 3 on the chart says to increase distances by 45 percent of the ground roll figure for a dry grass runway [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. So 0.45 x 605 = 272 feet is added to each: ground roll 605 + 272 = 877 feet, total 1,375 + 272 = 1,647 feet. Multiplying the total by 1.45 also inflates the air distance, which grass does not change; it shows the note was misread. 877 feet is the new ground roll, not the total. The paved number cannot be used as is: the conditions box says paved, level, dry runway and maximum braking [[1:456|PHAK A-4]], and chart data come from a new airplane flown with average skill [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. Teach her to read the conditions box and notes before any number.

questions.q: At a towered airport you are about to start a power-off 180 with a commercial learner. Her point is 700 feet past the threshold and today's POH ground roll is 605 feet. The tower offers a landing with a hold short of a crossing runway; the published Available Landing Distance is 1,450 feet. She wants to accept, because the POH total over a 50-foot obstacle is only 1,375 feet. What do you teach?
options: Accept: the 1,375-foot chart total is less than the 1,450-foot ALD, and that total already includes the air distance from the threshold to the touchdown
Decline now: the touchdown may be anywhere up to 200 feet past her point, so plan 700 + 200 + 605 = 1,505 feet, which is more than the 1,450-foot ALD
Accept: a LAHSO clearance does not rule out a rejected landing, so if the 180 runs long she can simply go around over the crossing runway
Decline, but only because LAHSO is used for instrument approaches; a VFR pilot flying an accuracy approach is never issued a hold-short clearance
questions.why: A pilot may accept LAHSO only after deciding the airplane can land and stop within the ALD [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]; the PIC has final authority to decline, and preflight planning should decide which combinations work [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. In this Task the touchdown may be anywhere from the point to 200 feet beyond it (ACS AI.VII.O.S8), so the distance to plan is 700 + 200 + 605 = 1,505 feet, more than 1,450. The chart total is measured from 50 feet over the threshold, but her touchdown is set by the point, not by the threshold. A LAHSO clearance does not preclude a rejected landing, but that is a backup, not a reason to accept; decline promptly, ideally before the clearance is issued [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. VFR pilots do receive LAHSO clearances.

questions.q: Your learner is in a steep forward slip on a power-off 180 final, flaps 20, trimmed for the glide, when a deer walks onto the runway. She calls "Going around" and shoves the throttle forward while still holding the slip. What order do you teach for a go-around out of a slip?
options: Power always comes first, so full throttle while still slipping is right; she can level the wings and center the rudder once the airplane is established in the climb at VY
Release the rudder sharply so the nose snaps straight, then bring all the flaps up at once to cut the drag, and only then add full power and set the climb attitude
Hold the slip and raise the nose to stop the sink, then add power slowly once the airspeed has built back up to VX, so the engine does not falter on the way
Level the wings and ease off the rudder together while setting the pitch, then full power smoothly, forward pressure, right rudder, flaps up in small steps
questions.why: The slip lesson's order: take the slip out first by leveling the wings and releasing the rudder while setting the pitch attitude [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], then full or maximum allowable power smoothly, forward pressure against the rising nose, right rudder, and flaps up in small steps after the descent stops [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Releasing the rudder abruptly swings the nose into line and the airplane picks up excess speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]; a sudden full flap retraction can let the airplane settle into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Trimmed for the glide, full power raises the nose sharply, the elevator trim stall setup [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and the airplane cannot climb below minimum power required speed, so raising the nose first without power is wrong [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Deer on the runway is the AIH's own teachable moment for always being ready to go around [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

questions.q: On a power-off 180 with the wind from the right, your learner is high on final and slips with the left wing low and right rudder. As she starts the round out she levels the wings to "take the slip out," and the airplane begins drifting left. What do you teach?
options: Her slip direction was fine, since either wing works in a slip; her only error was taking the slip out early, so next time she holds the slip all the way to the touchdown
Slip with the left wing low as she did, then at the round out reverse to the right wing low and left rudder, so the wind correction is set just before the touchdown
Skip the slip in a crosswind: bring up a notch of flaps to adjust the glide instead, and fly a crab all the way to the touchdown so the wings stay level
Slip with the right (upwind) wing low and left rudder; at the round out keep that wing down and use rudder to line up the nose: a sideslip to touchdown
questions.why: In a crosswind, lower the upwind wing so the slip is into the wind; that makes it easier to stay on the original path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. A slip in the same direction as the crosswind and a late transition to a sideslip are both listed errors [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. At the round out the forward slip comes out, but the upwind wing stays down and rudder aligns the nose: the wing-low method [[24:187|AFH 9-16]], with deflection increasing as speed decays [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. A downwind-wing slip forces a full control reversal at the worst moment, and leveling the wings leaves the airplane drifting. Holding a forward slip to the ground lands with the axis off the direction of motion, which side-loads the gear [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]. Never retract flaps to reach the spot [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

questions.q: Your learner closed the throttle late after a long downwind with a tailwind, and now she is low on base. She raises the nose below best glide speed and cracks the throttle "just a little" to make the point. What do you teach?
options: Raising the nose is right because it slows the descent; the throttle is the only error, so she keeps the nose up and leaves the power at idle from here to the round out
Below best glide, more nose-up makes the path much steeper; lower the nose to best glide, turn toward the runway early, hold the flaps, and go around if still short
The throttle is fine because the engine should be cleared now and then on a long glide; she just needs to add flaps sooner so the path stays steep enough
Add full flaps now and slip, because added drag slows the airplane, and a slower airplane always glides farther over the ground toward the point
questions.why: Below best glide, pitching up reduces airspeed and greatly steepens the descent angle, while pitching down shallows it [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], so a glide is never stretched [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. When short, the pilot may dog-leg toward the runway on base [[24:196|AFH 9-25]], and full flaps wait until adding them clearly will not put the landing short [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]; drag from flaps makes the glide steeper and shorter [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Clearing the engine is fine, but using the throttle to extend the glide is a listed error, as are stretching the glide and overextending the downwind with a tailwind [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. If there is any doubt the approach can be completed safely, go around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. Debrief where the energy went wrong: on downwind.

questions.q: Your learner enters a forward slip on final and the airspeed needle drops about 10 knots, though the nose has not moved. She pushes the nose down to bring the needle back. What do you teach?
options: Some airspeed indicators read badly in a slip because of where the pitot tube and static vents sit, so hold the pitch attitude you know and judge by sound and control feel
The needle is the primary airspeed reference in every phase, so lowering the nose was correct; she should just make the pitch change smaller and smoother next time
Take the slip out at once and add power, since a reading that low means the airplane is near a stall and the slip has made the stall warning unreliable
The low reading shows the slip is too steep for this airplane, so she should reduce the bank until the needle comes back up and then hold that bank
questions.why: Because of the location of the pitot tube and static vents, airspeed indicators in some airplanes may have considerable error in a slip; the pilot should recognize a properly done slip by attitude, the sound of the airflow and the feel of the controls, and controls airspeed with the elevator [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Reacting to erroneous airspeed indications is a listed slip error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Pushing over to chase the needle builds real airspeed, so she arrives fast and floats. Bank sets the amount of slip and the sink rate [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], not the reading, so taking bank out to fix the needle gives up the descent she wanted. Show her the displaced reading at altitude first, so it does not surprise her in the pattern.

questions.q: Your airplane's POH limits slips to a set time to prevent fuel starvation. On a long final in a steady crosswind, your learner flies wing-low for over a minute and says the limit only covers forward slips. Another learner insists 30 seconds is the FAA limit for all single-engine airplanes. What do you teach?
options: The first learner is right: the limit is about the yaw of a forward slip, and in a sideslip the nose stays on the runway, so the fuel stays where it belongs in the tank
The second learner is right: 30 seconds is the limit for every single-engine airplane, so after 30 seconds of wing-low she must change to a crab and hold it
A long wing-low final is a slip too, so the POH limit counts there; 30 seconds is only the AFH's example, so brief the number in this airplane's POH
Both are wrong: the limit matters only in a real engine failure, when fuel may be low; in practice with full tanks no slip limit applies at all
questions.why: Some airplanes limit slips in duration or by fuel quantity, to prevent fuel starvation when fuel is forced to one side of a tank in uncoordinated flight [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. The AFH's multiengine chapter adds that some single-engine airplanes have POH limits on slips beyond a set time, giving 30 seconds only as an example, and says the limit should be observed with the wing-low method too [[24:271|AFH 13-22]]. So the POH number is the rule, not 30 seconds. Saying the limit matters only in a real failure has it backward: in a real engine-out slip to a field, the AFH says the time or fuel limit is irrelevant unless a prolonged slip caused the problem [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

questions.q: On a normal approach your learner passes 250 feet AGL 15 knots fast and descending about 1,100 fpm. She says, "I've got it, I'll pull the power and float it off; the runway is long." What do you teach?
options: Let her try: the AFH says to focus on the elements of a stable approach rather than meet every criterion, and the long runway gives her room to float it off
Go around now: an approach that becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL calls for an immediate go-around, and the urge to save it is landing expectancy
Let her continue, but have her slip to kill the speed, since a forward slip loses altitude without gaining airspeed and fixes the speed and the sink at once
Take the controls and land it yourself, since a go-around this low is riskier than a fast landing, then debrief the stabilized criteria on the ground
questions.why: The AFH criteria want airspeed within +10/-5 knots of the landing speed and a descent rate generally 500 to 1,000 fpm, reduced before 300 feet AGL, and in a typical GA pattern an immediate go-around if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Focusing on elements, not every criterion, is advice for setting up the approach, not a waiver of that gate. Excess speed also costs runway, about 20 percent more distance for 10 percent more speed [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. A slip adds sink she already has too much of. A go-around is a normal maneuver, not proof of poor skill [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]; it is dangerous only when delayed, and delay comes from landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Let her fly it so she learns the call.

questions.q: After a go-around at a nontowered field, your learner climbs to 500 feet AGL over midfield and starts a turn to crosswind to get back into the pattern quickly. Pattern altitude is 1,000 feet AGL. What do you teach?
options: Turning early is fine at a nontowered field, because the rules set only the direction of turns, and it cuts the time she spends low and slow after the go-around
Climb straight ahead to pattern altitude, then turn crosswind wherever she is, and skip the before-landing checklist since gear and flaps were set on the last lap
Make a teardrop turn back to downwind at 500 feet to stay close to the runway, and announce on the CTAF that she is re-entering the pattern
Go straight past the departure end, turn crosswind beyond it and within 300 feet of pattern altitude, and redo the before-landing checklist on downwind
questions.why: After a takeoff or go-around, continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end of the runway, staying aware of pattern traffic, and turn crosswind only beyond the departure end and within 300 feet below pattern altitude [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]] [[1:355|PHAK 14-21]]. At 500 feet AGL she is 500 feet below a 1,000-foot pattern. Following the standard pattern also avoids excessive maneuvering at low altitude [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. The go-around broke the normal pattern flow, so the before-landing checklist is done again on the new downwind; that is the habit that keeps the gear down [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

questions.q: On a short-field landing to a 100-foot box, your learner crosses the threshold 8 knots fast with full flaps and the airplane floats past her point. She keeps holding it off, planning to touch down late and stand on the brakes. What do you teach?
options: Touch down and brake hard: maximum braking right after touchdown is the short-field technique, and it makes up for the float as long as the tires do not lock
Push the nose down to put the wheels on near the point, since a firm touchdown beats a long float and the nosewheel can take the load at this speed
Go around: full power smoothly, forward pressure against the nose-up trim and right rudder, then flaps up in small steps once the descent has stopped
Go around: full power and bring all the flaps up at once to cut the drag, then pitch up to VX right away to get the airplane clear of the ground quickly
questions.why: Excess speed causes floating, and prolonged floating should be avoided, especially on short runways; if it cannot land in the first third, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. A long touchdown can make the calculated landing distance impossible to achieve [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]], and failing to recognize and abort a poor approach is on the short-field error list [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. The go-around: full power smoothly, expect the nose to rise and yaw left and hold forward pressure and right rudder, flaps up in small steps after the descent stops [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; with flaps and nose-up trim, pitch forces change a lot [[24:235|AFH 12-4]]. All flaps up at once can settle the airplane, and climbing out of ground effect too early may leave it unable to climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Forcing it on with forward pressure invites wheelbarrowing [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

questions.q: A large twin turboprop lands ahead of you on the same 3,000-foot runway and touches down about 1,500 feet from the threshold. Your learner is set up for a short-field landing with her point 300 feet down the runway. What do you teach?
options: Stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point; if that leaves too little runway for her stop, wait or use another runway
Land on her point as planned: a short-field landing touches down far short of the turboprop's touchdown point, so she stays well below its vortices
Land on her point, but only once ATC has given a wake turbulence caution; without one, the controller has already provided the spacing she needs
Fly a steeper approach under its path and touch down early, because vortices sink and drift off the runway and are gone by the time she lands
questions.why: Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway: stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Vortices form from rotation to touchdown and sink, and near the ground drift sideways only 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]], so landing short of its touchdown point puts her under them. Whether or not ATC gives a warning, the pilot is expected to adjust the flight path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]], and the pilot is ultimately responsible for an appropriate interval [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Here beyond 1,500 feet leaves about 1,500 feet of runway; work the chart before deciding. The AIM gives no short-field exception.

questions.q: Your learner's short-field chart gives 1,550 feet to clear 50 feet. Her personal rule is a 20 percent margin over calculated takeoff distance. The strip is 1,800 feet with trees off the end. She says, "1,550 against 1,800 leaves 250 to spare: go." What do you teach?
options: With her margin, 1,550 x 1.2 = 1,860 feet, more than the 1,800-foot strip, so it is a no-go for her today; the chart also assumes a new airplane and average skill
She is right: the chart is already conservative because it assumes a new airplane and average skill, so a personal margin on top only applies at night or in rain
With her margin only the ground roll grows 20 percent, which still fits inside the 1,800 feet, so it is a go as long as she lifts off before midfield
It is a go if she climbs 5 knots below VX, because the slower speed steepens the climb enough to make up the distance her margin takes away
questions.why: With a 20 percent factor, 1,550 x 1.2 = 1,860 feet, which exceeds 1,800, just like the RMH pilot whose 4,700 feet became 5,640 feet against a 5,000-foot runway [[30:36|RMH 4-3]]. Factoring performance data to create safety margins is an RMH risk mitigation [[30:39|RMH 5-1]], and takeoffs grow more hazardous as calculated performance approaches the available runway [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Chart data assume a new airplane and average skill, so they are not conservative; adjust for a worn airplane or weaker technique [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. Personal minimums are not adjusted to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Flying below the POH speed risks a stall, poor control or a very low initial climb [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]], and in some airplanes 5 knots costs a lot of climb [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

questions.q: On a short-field takeoff the airplane starts to get light well before VX. Worried about flying below VX, your learner pushes forward to pin the nosewheel on until VX. What do you teach?
options: Pinning it is right: the ACS wants VX after lift-off, so she should hold forward pressure, adding more if the nose still tries to come up early
Let it fly and climb at once at the VX attitude, since getting away from the runway early is worth more than the few knots it is still missing
Reject the takeoff, since an airplane that wants to fly early points to a weight and balance error that will make the VX climb unsafe
Let it lift off, level off with the wheels just clear and accelerate in ground effect to VX; pinning it can cause wheelbarrowing
questions.why: When an airplane becomes airborne before VX, the AFH says to let it lift off, then reduce pitch to level until it accelerates to VX with the wheels just clear of the runway. That is preferable to forcing it to stay on the ground with forward elevator pressure, which overloads the nosewheel, may cause wheelbarrowing and hinders acceleration [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Wheelbarrowing lets the airplane swerve or pivot on the nosewheel [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. Climbing out of ground effect below the recommended speed gives much less climb than VY or even VX [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

questions.q: On a short-field takeoff with a simulated 50-foot obstacle, your learner holds VX up to 400 feet AGL "for safety" before lowering the nose. What do you teach?
options: Holding VX longer is the safer habit, since the steeper climb puts more height between the airplane and the ground if the engine quits before pattern altitude
At 50 feet, or once past the named obstacle, lower the nose slightly to VY; VX is slow and nose-high, so an engine failure there needs a bigger, quicker push
She should hold VX until the gear and flaps are up, then lower the nose to VY, because the airplane must be cleaned up before it is allowed to accelerate
The ACS lets her choose VX or VY all the way to a safe maneuvering altitude, so either is correct as long as she holds the one she picks within 5 knots
questions.why: Your standard: VX ±5 knots until the obstacle is cleared or until 50 feet AGL if simulating, then VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS AI.VII.E.S10, S11, S13). The AFH flies VX to the obstacle or 50 feet, lowers the pitch slightly to VY, and retracts gear and flaps at a stable VY [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. VX often sits just above stall speed [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]], and at a climb attitude without power the airplane is at or near a stalling angle of attack, so the nose must come down at once [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. A steep climb also hides traffic over the nose [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

questions.q: On a normal takeoff with a left crosswind, your learner starts with full left aileron and holds it there the whole roll. At lift-off the airplane banks steeply left. What do you teach?
options: Start with the aileron neutral and add it only when the upwind wing starts to rise, because aileron held early in the roll adds drag and lengthens the run
Keep the full aileron as she did, but lift off a few knots slower, so the bank at lift-off has less airspeed behind it and stays smaller
Full aileron at brake release is right; as speed builds, ease it to just what keeps the wings level, keeping some in, and judge drift from the runway
Keep the full aileron as she did, but add right rudder at lift-off to level the wings, since rudder is the main roll control at low airspeed
questions.why: Start the roll with full aileron into the wind [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]; less than full aileron at the start is a listed error. As speed builds, use just enough aileron to keep the wings level while still holding some in the whole roll [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. Holding a fixed amount is the listed error of mechanical aileron use rather than judging lateral position from visual cues, and too much aileron late leaves a steep bank into the wind at lift-off [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. The deflected controls do add drag [[24:138|AFH 6-6]], but neutral aileron lets the upwind wing rise and the airplane skip. In a significant crosswind the AFH holds the mains on slightly longer, then a definite lift-off [[24:139|AFH 6-7]], not a slower one.

questions.q: Thunderstorms are building about 10 miles from the field. On the takeoff roll your learner sees the airspeed come up slower than usual, then a gust pushes it up. She keeps going. What do you teach?
options: Continue: a gust that raises the airspeed shows the wind is helping, and lifting off a little early gets the airplane up and away from the ground sooner
Continue, but lower the nose right after lift-off to rebuild airspeed if it falls, since holding VY within a few knots is the standard she has been trained to
Slow acceleration is a reason to reject; on the roll it may be the only sign of windshear, and gusts can hide it, so stop and wait the storms out on the ground
Continue, but climb at VX instead of VY, because the steeper climb takes the airplane above the windshear layer in the shortest possible time
questions.why: Low-level windshear comes with thunderstorms and fronts and is worst near the ground [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the runway the only indication may be a slower-than-normal airspeed increase, and gusts can mask it [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. Inadequate acceleration is a reason to reject a takeoff [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. In the studied accidents pilots lowered the nose to regain airspeed and lost altitude; recovery needs holding or raising pitch and accepting lower airspeed [[28:267|AWH 22-12]], the habit your airspeed drills can undo. Some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]], so the real defense is waiting on the ground.

questions.q: Briefing the engine-failure plan before a normal takeoff, your learner says that if the engine quits at 300 feet AGL she will make a standard-rate turn back to the runway behind her. What do you teach?
options: Lower the nose at once, center the rudder and land about straight ahead; the FAA's 300-foot turn-back example ends about 1,016 feet below the runway
A turn back works if she banks steeply, about 45 degrees, to keep the turn short, so the brief should call for a steep turn instead of a standard-rate one
A turn back is fine from 300 feet for any pilot, so she should climb at VX after every takeoff to reach 300 feet over the runway sooner
Hold the climb attitude while she trims for the glide, since keeping the nose up saves altitude while she decides which way to turn
questions.why: At a climb pitch without power the airplane is at or near a stalling angle of attack, maybe with right rudder still held: lower the nose at once, center the rudder and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. The AFH example from 300 feet AGL, with 4 seconds to react and a standard-rate turn, ends 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]], and a turn back is an unacceptable risk for student, low-time and untrained pilots [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. A steep turn near a stall that low is the stall/spin setup: 60 percent of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

questions.q: Your learner's POH approach speed is 65 knots. The wind is down the runway at 14 knots gusting 24. Using the common half-gust-factor practice, what speed does she fly, and what window does your CFI ACS hold you to when you demonstrate it?
options: 75 knots, adding the full 10-knot gust factor, flown within +10/-5 knots, the same window the AFH stabilized-approach criteria use
70 knots, adding half of the 10-knot gust factor, flown ±5 knots (65 to 75 knots), with some power held until the main wheels touch
77 knots, adding half of the 24-knot gust to 65, flown ±5 knots, with the throttle closed early so the airplane does not float in the gusts
65 knots with nothing added, since the headwind already lowers the groundspeed, flown ±5 knots, with full flaps for the steepest path
questions.why: The gust factor is 24 - 14 = 10 knots; half of it is 5, so 65 + 5 = 70 knots. The AFH example is the same method: 70 knots normal with 15-knot gusts gives 77 [[24:191|AFH 9-20]], which is where the 77 trap comes from. Your standard is ±5 knots with gust factor applied (ACS AI.VII.B.S7), so 65 to 75 knots. The AFH stabilized criteria allow +10/-5 [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], but that is not your checkride window. In turbulence use a power-on approach, partial flaps in a gusty crosswind, and close the throttle only after the mains touch, since chopping it early can drop the airplane [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

questions.q: On final your learner's aiming point is slowly sliding down the windshield, away from the horizon, and the runway looks long and narrow. She is on speed with power at idle and flaps 20. She says, "We're a bit low, I'll hold what I have." What do you teach?
options: She is low: add power and raise the nose to stop the descent until the aiming point stops moving, then rejoin the path toward the aiming point
She is high: push the nose over toward the point to steepen the path, since a dive gets her back onto the glide path faster than adding drag does
She is on path: an aiming point that slides down the windshield is normal as the airplane gets closer, so she holds what she has and waits
She is high and will land past the point: power is at idle, so add drag with more flaps or a forward slip while the elevator holds speed
questions.why: If the aiming point moves down away from the horizon, the airplane will land beyond it, and a runway that looks longer and narrower means the approach is steep [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Too high: lower the nose and reduce power and add flaps if available [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; with power already at idle, drag is what is left. A forward slip steepens the path while holding approach speed, and diving builds a sink rate where 800 to 1,000 fpm is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. In the slip, the elevator controls airspeed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Ask her to read the picture aloud before she touches anything; she named the wrong error.

questions.q: Your learner keeps rounding out too high and then dropping in. In the flare her eyes stay fixed on the runway just past the nose. What is the likely cause, and what do you teach?
options: Focusing too far down the runway makes her misjudge height, so she should look only at the near end of the runway, just over the nose, all through the flare
Rounding out high comes from too little back pressure, so she should start the flare at about 50 feet to give herself more time to bring the nose up
Rounding out high comes from carrying power, so she should close the throttle well before the round out so that the airplane settles sooner
Focusing too close blurs the reference, so she over-controls and rounds out high; move her focus slowly from over the nose to the touchdown zone and back
questions.why: Focusing too close to the airplane gives a too-high round out, and too far a too-low one [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Close focus blurs the reference, so the pilot over-controls, rounds out high and drops in; the fix is a natural head position with focus moving slowly from just over the nose to the touchdown zone and back, and peripheral vision judging height [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. The round out normally starts at about 10 to 20 feet [[24:179|AFH 9-8]], not 50. When she does round out high, hold the attitude until the airplane starts to settle, with a little power if needed [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

questions.q: At a towered airport you and a learner are holding short of a turf runway for a soft-field takeoff. The tower says, "Line up and wait." What do you teach her to do?
options: Read it back, roll on and keep moving into the takeoff, since a soft-field takeoff is not supposed to stop and the tower expects the airplane to roll
Read it back, line up and stop with the yoke back and power up, then start the roll as soon as the traffic on final has landed and cleared
Tell the tower she is unable, since stopping on the soft surface could bog the airplane down, and hold short until she is cleared for takeoff
Read it back, then line up and stop briefly with the brakes held to run the before-takeoff checklist, which the rolling soft-field lineup leaves out
questions.why: Line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]], and ATC should be told at once if there is any doubt about the ability to comply with an instruction [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]]. On a soft surface the airplane is kept moving while lining up, because stopping in mud or snow might bog it down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. So she holds short and says unable. Rolling without a takeoff clearance is a pilot deviation. The before-takeoff checklist is finished before taxiing onto the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], with the airplane stopped [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]], so nothing is left for the runway.

questions.q: Heavy and on a warm day, your learner lifts off a soft strip and right away climbs to about 30 feet, below VX. The stall horn chirps, the airplane mushes, and full power is not making it climb. What is happening, and what do you teach?
options: She left ground effect too slow, so induced drag rose and the airplane is in the region of reversed command; lower the nose, accepting some height loss, to regain speed
It is a power problem: lean the mixture for best power and raise the flaps all at once to cut drag, which lets the airplane accelerate without losing height
The airplane needs more lift: add back pressure to raise the angle of attack and hold the nose high until the climb rate comes back on its own
Ground effect is pushing the nose down, so hold the pitch attitude where it is and wait, since the airplane will climb once it is clear of ground effect
questions.why: Climbing out of ground effect before reaching normal climb pitch and airspeed can put the airplane in the region of reversed command at a low altitude, unable to climb even at full power; the only fix is to lower the nose, which costs altitude [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Leaving ground effect needs more angle of attack and brings more induced drag and a pitch-up tendency [[24:142|AFH 6-10]], and hot, heavy airplanes may not climb out at all [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. That is why it must stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. More back pressure deepens the problem. Flaps come up in increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift and settling [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

questions.q: Your learner makes a good soft-field touchdown on a muddy strip, then pushes the yoke forward to get the nosewheel down for steering and taps the brakes to slow down. What do you teach?
options: That is fine once the mains are down: weight on the nosewheel gives steering, and light braking shortens the rollout on a soft surface without loading the nose
Keep back pressure to hold the nosewheel off until the elevator loses effectiveness, ease it down with a touch of power, no brakes, and keep rolling to firm ground
Hold the nosewheel off, then stop on the runway with the brakes once the nose is down, so she can raise the flaps before taxiing on through the mud
Lower the nosewheel at once and hold forward pressure, but skip the brakes; the mud will slow the airplane, and nosewheel steering keeps it straight
questions.why: Hold enough back pressure to keep the nosewheel off, and lower it gently; a slight addition of power usually helps. Brakes are not needed on a soft field and should be avoided, since they load the nose gear and can make the nosewheel dig in, and the airplane is kept moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Your standard is to keep the nosewheel off until loss of elevator effectiveness (ACS AI.VII.D.S9). Flaps stay down on the rollout [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. Weight on the nosewheel at speed lets the airplane swerve or pivot on it [[24:206|AFH 9-35]], and stopping in mud can bog it down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Name the habit: it is the normal-landing rollout coming back.

questions.q: On a soft-field landing with a light right crosswind, your learner floats a foot off the runway with some power on, then raises the nose too fast and the airplane balloons about 10 feet. Speed is decaying and it starts to drift left. What do you teach?
options: Go around: full power smoothly, keep the right wing down, stop the nose from rising too far, stay low while speed builds, then flaps up in small steps once climbing
Close the throttle so the airplane settles back quickly, then hold the nosewheel off, since the soft surface will absorb a firmer touchdown than pavement would
Push the nose down to get back into ground effect, then hold that lower attitude and land on all three wheels so the nosewheel steering stops the drift
Go around: full power and pull up to VX right away to get clear of the ground and the drift, then bring the flaps up all at once so it climbs faster
questions.why: A large balloon calls for a go-around, with power before the stall, and if the airplane starts to drift after a balloon the AFH also says go around; the wing must be lowered further because the slower airplane drifts more [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]. Until the nosewheel is down, a soft-field landing can still become a takeoff [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Do not pitch up for a climb without airspeed, and bring the flaps up in small increments [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; climbing out of ground effect too early may leave the airplane unable to climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Closing the throttle quickly brings a jump in sink rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. A fast three-wheel touchdown with forward pressure is the classic wheelbarrowing cause [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].
